demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette: Arjun Mehta had been the overnight floor supervisor at a downtown Marriott for twelve years when the incident on the grand staircase shattered his routine. He was stripping the marble lobby, rushing to finish before the morning conference check-in, convinced his regional manager was watching from the mezzanine. In his hurry to buff a stubborn stain near the top step, he applied an industrial degreaser too heavily. When he turned to load the wax machine, an elderly businessman stepped onto the freshly treated patch. Arjun heard the sickening crack and the man's sharp cry. By the time Arjun dropped his buffer and scrambled down, the man's leg was already twisted at an unnatural angle, blood soaking through his trousers. The paramedics called it a severe comminuted fracture. Arjun called it his fault. He had been reckless. He had prioritized speed over safety. He had broken the unspoken rule of his faith and his culture: to provide and protect, not to cause harm. In the weeks that followed, Arjun's shifts became a minefield. The polished lobby floor no longer gleamed; it glared. Sometimes, while folding linen carts in the staff laundry room, a sudden draft would stir the chemical scent of industrial degreaser, and without any gradual build-up, the lobby would flash in his mind as a series of frozen frames: the gleaming marble, the man's falling body, the shattered hip. Each snapshot was accompanied by a heat that crawled up his neck and tightened into a hot, impotent rage. He didn't know how to stop it. A spilled mop bucket or the squeak of a housekeeping cart could instantly summon the memory, leaving him gripping a supply cart until his knuckles whitened. These sudden intrusions soon bled into his core beliefs. He had come to believe that every time the memory struck, it pulled him downward into a certainty that he was fundamentally broken. What frightened him most was how quickly the flash cemented his conviction that he had violated the very values he had spent a lifetime upholding. The self-reproach was absolute; he told himself the injury happened solely because of his own negligence, his own inability to stay present. As the flashes repeated, the conviction deepened until the world outside his shift felt utterly hollow. He could not see purpose in his routine, nor in the empty house he returned to after his divorce. The memories did not just recall the past; they directly forged his belief that he was irredeemable and that nothing in his life held any meaning. Over months, the link between the flashes and his self-condemnation only hardened. He began arriving hours early, staying late, and avoiding the ground floor entirely. He requested transfers to the upper floors, then eventually to the back-loading docks, where the concrete was always damp and the chemical smells were masked by diesel. His supervisor noted his growing isolation and the way he flinched at the sound of rolling carts. Every time the memory intruded, the self-blame followed with immediate force, leaving him convinced that his values were shattered and his life devoid of meaning. This certainty deepened his isolation. He avoided colleagues and his ex-wife, telling himself that anyone who knew what he did would see him as a danger. Last month, while refilling a supply closet on the forty-second floor, the sharp hiss of a pressurized steam cleaner triggered the full sensory recall. Arjun dropped a box of cleaning supplies and sank to his knees, his breath catching in a panic attack. He was finally referred to occupational health. Now, sitting in the counselor's office, Arjun is terrified of being fired and dragged back to the lobby. What he hopes for, though quietly, is to find a way to carry the weight without it crushing him, to stop the rage from dictating his mornings, and to believe, even for a moment, that he might deserve to keep going.
